frugal

/FROO-gul/ — stress on the first syllable · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Someone who is frugal is careful and economical with money, spending only what is necessary and avoiding waste.

A frugal traveler, he cooked hostel dinners instead of eating out.

Example

On a backpacking trip across Southeast Asia, Marcus stayed frugal: he ate street food, took overnight buses to save on hotels, and wore the same clothes repeatedly rather than buying new items.

Frugal is more precise than 'careful with money' here because it captures not just being careful but actively choosing the cheaper option and avoiding waste — Marcus isn't just budgeting; he's committed to spending only what is necessary.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

stingy: Stingy means unwilling to spend money or share what you have, and it always sounds like an insult. Frugal is a compliment by comparison: a frugal person spends carefully on purpose, avoiding waste but still paying for what truly matters. Stinginess hoards; a frugal person manages.

sparing: Sparing means using or giving something only in small amounts — you can be sparing with salt or with praise, one situation at a time. Frugal is bigger than any single moment: a whole disciplined habit of spending as little money as possible and wasting nothing.

prudent: Prudent means careful and sensible about the future — a prudent choice weighs the risks before acting, whether or not money is involved. Frugal is specifically about spending: a frugal person keeps costs low and avoids waste. Buying good insurance is prudent; packing leftovers for lunch is frugal.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

extravagant: spending far more than is needed

lavish: giving or spending very freely

Where it sits · how disciplined the saving is

wasteful → economical → thrifty → frugal

wasteful vs. frugal: Wasteful sits at the opposite end of the scale from frugal, spending carelessly on things that aren't needed.

economical vs. frugal: Economical means using resources efficiently, while frugal goes further — a deliberate, disciplined habit of saving.

thrifty vs. frugal: Thrifty means clever about saving money, and frugal intensifies that into a whole lifestyle of avoiding waste.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — frug-: fruit, produce, profit (so 'useful, worth something') (Latin (frux, frugis))

Suffix — -al: relating to, characteristic of (Latin (-alis))

Put it together: Frug- comes from Latin frux, 'fruit, produce, profit,' plus -al, 'relating to' — being frugal originally meant handling money and resources so they bear fruit instead of going to waste.

Use the root in a new word: fruitful: Their weekend of studying proved fruitful: both friends aced the exam.

Strength Check

Word Choice

neutral

Use frugal when someone is genuinely committed to avoiding unnecessary spending and waste — it's a lifestyle choice, not just a temporary measure. For simple efficiency with resources, economical is the clearer choice.
